questions.q: A Stone Age family counts its goats by keeping one stick for each goat. Which statement about this method is correct?
questions.a: It can be used for any number of goats, but it needs as many sticks as there are goats
o: It can be used for any number of goats, but it needs as many sticks as there are goats
It can count at most 26 goats, because it uses the letters of the alphabet

questions.q: What are the symbols used in a written number system called? Give one example of such a symbol from the Hindu number system.
questions.a: They are called numerals. For example 0, 5, 36 or 193 are numerals of the Hindu number system.
s: Names the written symbols as numerals
Gives a correct example from the Hindu number system, such as 0, 5, 36 or 193

questions.q: A herder keeps one stick for each cow in her herd and has no number names. (a) At the gate she matches every returning cow with one stick. After the last cow, two sticks are left over. What does this tell her? (b) What is this way of matching each cow with exactly one stick, so that no two cows share a stick, called? (c) Name one standard sequence that does not use physical objects and that can also be used for counting.
questions.a: (a) Two cows have not returned. (b) A one-to-one mapping. (c) A sequence of sounds or names (such as the letters of a language), or a sequence of written symbols (such as the Roman numerals).
s: (a) Says that two cows have not returned, since two sticks have no cow
(b) Names it a one-to-one mapping
(c) Gives a standard sequence of sounds or names, or of written symbols

questions.q: A class extends the letter method of counting like this: a, b, c, ..., z stand for 1 to 26, and then aa, bb, cc, ..., zz stand for 27 to 52, in that order. Which number does 'ff' stand for, and which string stands for 45?
questions.a: ff stands for 32, and 45 is written ss
o: ff stands for 32, and 45 is written ss
ff stands for 32, and 45 is written rr
ff stands for 33, and 45 is written ss
ff stands for 12, and 45 is written ss

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The sounds of the letters a to z cannot be used to count a collection of 40 objects.
Reason (R): The sequence of the 26 letters comes to an end, so it is not an unending standard sequence.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

questions.q: A teacher says a good number system must (i) be an unending standard sequence and (ii) be convenient to count with. Say whether each method meets (i) and (ii): (a) keeping one stick for each object, (b) saying the letters a to z in order, (c) writing the Roman symbols I, II, III, IV, V, ... in order.
questions.a: (a) It is unending, but it is not convenient for large collections because it needs as many sticks as objects. (b) It is convenient, but it is not unending because it stops at the 26th letter. (c) It is convenient, but it is not unending because arbitrarily large numbers need more and more new symbols.
s: (a) Sticks: unending but not convenient for large collections
(b) Letters: convenient but not unending (ends at 26)
(c) Roman symbols: convenient but not unending (more and more symbols needed)

questions.q: True or false: A collection is counted by making a one-to-one mapping between its objects and a standard sequence, taken in the order of the sequence. Give the reason or the correct statement.
questions.a: True. Each object is matched with the next item of the standard sequence in order, so the last item reached tells the size of the collection.
s: States the verdict: True
Gives the reason: each object takes the next item of the fixed-order sequence, and the last item reached gives the size

questions.q:
A shepherd boy in a hill village has no number names. Each morning, as his goats leave the pen one by one, he says the letters of the English alphabet in their fixed order, one letter for each goat. On Monday the last goat to leave gets the letter r. In the evening he does the same as the goats come back, and the last goat to return gets the letter p. His neighbour keeps one stick for each of her goats instead.
(a) How many goats left the pen on Monday morning?
(b) How many goats did not come back that evening?
(c) Next week he buys 11 more goats. Can he still count the whole herd as they leave in the morning? Give a reason.
(d) Give one advantage of his letter method over the neighbour's sticks, and one advantage of the sticks over his letters.
questions.a: (a) r is the 18th letter, so 18 goats left. (b) p is the 16th letter, so 16 came back and 18 - 16 = 2 goats did not come back. (c) No. The herd becomes 18 + 11 = 29 goats, but the letters end at z, the 26th, so the last 3 goats get no letter. (d) The letters are convenient: he does not need to carry as many sticks as goats. The sticks form an unending standard sequence, so they never run out, however large the herd grows.
s: (a) Finds that r stands for 18 goats
(b) Finds 16 returned and 2 did not come back
(c) Says no: 29 goats but only 26 letters
(d) Gives convenience for letters and an unending sequence for sticks

questions.q:
Tara keeps one stick for each of her cows, and she has 15 sticks. Her neighbour has 22 sticks.
(a) Who has fewer cows?
(b) How many more cows does Tara need to have as many as her neighbour?
(c) One evening 13 cows walk back and Tara matches each with one stick. How many cows have not returned?
(d) Tara ties her 15 sticks into bundles of 5. How many bundles does she make?
(e) After getting the cows in part (b), how many bundles of 5 and how many loose sticks does she have?
questions.a: (a) Tara has fewer cows, since 15 is less than 22. (b) 22 - 15 = 7 more cows. (c) 15 - 13 = 2 cows have not returned. (d) 15 / 5 = 3 bundles. (e) She then has 22 sticks, which makes 4 bundles of 5 and 2 loose sticks.
s: (a) Says Tara, since 15 is less than 22
(b) Finds 22 - 15 = 7 more cows
(c) Finds 15 - 13 = 2 cows not returned
(d) Finds 3 bundles of 5
(e) Finds 4 bundles and 2 loose sticks for 22 sticks

questions.q: Which tally bone, found in South Africa, has 29 notches and is about 44,000 years old?
questions.a: The Lebombo bone

questions.q: In the Gumulgal number system of Australia, urapon stands for 1 and ukasar stands for 2. Which number is named ukasar-ukasar-ukasar?

questions.a: Q, with 10 symbols and marks
o: Q and R, with 11 symbols and marks each

questions.q: A person tallying with one mark per object decides to replace every group of 5 marks by a new symbol. Give two reasons why this helps.
questions.a: Most people cannot see at a glance a group of 5 or more objects, so a group of 5 marks is hard to read. A single symbol for 5 marks makes the record shorter and easier to read than a long row of single marks.
s: Says that a group of 5 or more marks cannot be read at a glance
Says that one symbol for a group makes the record shorter and easier to read

questions.q: In the Gumulgal number system urapon is 1 and ukasar is 2. Write the Gumulgal names for the numbers 4 and 5.
questions.a: 4 is ukasar-ukasar, since 4 = 2 + 2. 5 is ukasar-ukasar-urapon, since 5 = 2 + 2 + 1.
s: Writes 4 as ukasar-ukasar
Writes 5 as ukasar-ukasar-urapon

questions.q: (a) In which country was the Lebombo bone discovered? (b) It has 29 notches. In a tally, what does each notch stand for? (c) Name one thing the bone may have been used as.
questions.a: (a) South Africa. (b) Each notch stands for one object that was counted. (c) It may have been a tally stick, or a lunar calendar.
s: (a) Names South Africa
(b) Says each notch stands for one counted object
(c) Names a tally stick or a lunar calendar

Assertion (A): The Gumulgal, Bakairi and Bushmen developed equivalent number systems.

questions.q:
Three herders record the same flock of 47 goats. Asha keeps one tally mark for each goat. Binu uses a symbol for each group of 10 goats and a mark for each goat left over. Chetan uses a symbol for each group of 20 goats, then a symbol for each group of 5 goats from what is left, and a mark for each goat left after that.
(a) How many symbols and marks are in Binu's record?
(b) How many symbols and marks are in Chetan's record?
(c) Can a reader see at a glance how many loose marks there are in Binu's record? Give a reason.
(d) Whose record is the easiest to read, and why?
questions.a: (a) 47 = 4 tens + 7, so Binu has 4 symbols and 7 marks, 11 in all. (b) 47 = 2 x 20 + 1 x 5 + 2, so Chetan has 2 + 1 + 2 = 5 symbols and marks. (c) No. Binu has 7 loose marks, and most people find it difficult to count 5 or more objects in a single glance. (d) Chetan's record: it is the shortest (5 against 11 and 47), and no bunch in it has 5 or more of the same mark, so every part can be read at a glance.
s: (a) Finds 4 symbols and 7 marks, 11 in all
(b) Groups 47 as 2 twenties, 1 five and 2 marks, 5 in all
(c) Says no, since 7 marks is more than can be seen at a glance
(d) Chooses Chetan's record: fewest marks and no bunch of 5 or more

questions.q:
A bone has 87 notches, one for each object counted. A scribe rewrites the count by replacing every complete group of 5 notches by one symbol P.
(a) How many P symbols and how many loose notches are there?
(b) How many marks are there now altogether?
(c) How many fewer marks is that than the original 87 notches?
(d) The scribe now also replaces every complete group of 5 P symbols by a new symbol Q. How many Q symbols, P symbols and loose notches are there?
(e) How many marks are there now, and how many fewer than the original 87?
questions.a: (a) 87 = 17 x 5 + 2, so 17 P symbols and 2 loose notches. (b) 17 + 2 = 19 marks. (c) 87 - 19 = 68 fewer. (d) 17 = 3 x 5 + 2, so 3 Q symbols, 2 P symbols and 2 loose notches. (e) 3 + 2 + 2 = 7 marks, which is 87 - 7 = 80 fewer than the original.
s: (a) Finds 17 P symbols and 2 loose notches
(b) Finds 19 marks
(c) Finds 68 fewer marks
(d) Finds 3 Q symbols, 2 P symbols and 2 loose notches
(e) Finds 7 marks and 80 fewer than 87

questions.q: A Roman clerk writes 49 with the shorter forms, as XLIX. An older clerk never uses the shorter forms: he groups 49 into as many 10s as possible, then 5s, then 1s. How many more symbols does the older clerk write?

questions.q: Write 2352 in Roman numerals by grouping it into landmark numbers, largest first. How many symbols does the numeral have?

questions.q: Add CLXXVI and CLXXXII without converting them to Hindu numerals. (a) Collect the like symbols. (b) Regroup them from the largest landmark number. (c) Write the sum.
questions.a: (a) Together there are 2 C, 2 L, 5 X, 1 V and 3 I. (b) 2 L make 1 C, so there are 3 C; 5 X make 1 L; so the symbols are 3 C, 1 L, 1 V and 3 I. (c) The sum is CCCLVIII.

(b) Regroups 2 L into 1 C and 5 X into 1 L

questions.q: True or false: In the Roman system, the product of any two landmark numbers is always another landmark number. Give the reason or the correct statement.
questions.a: False. For example V x L = 5 x 50 = 250, which is CCL, and 250 is not a Roman landmark number.
s: States the verdict: False
Gives a counter-example such as V x L = CCL, which is not a landmark number

questions.q:
Without converting to Hindu numerals, multiply XXIII by XII.
(a) Split each numeral into its landmark numbers.
(b) Multiply every part of XXIII by every part of XII and list the products.
(c) Collect the like symbols.
(d) Regroup them, largest landmark number first.
(e) Write the product.
questions.a: (a) XXIII = X + X + I + I + I and XII = X + I + I. (b) Each X of XXIII times XII gives C + X + X, and each I of XXIII times XII gives X + I + I. (c) Collecting, there are 2 C, 7 X and 6 I. (d) 7 X make L and XX, and 6 I make V and I, so the symbols are 2 C, 1 L, 2 X, 1 V and 1 I. (e) The product is CCLXXVI.
s: (a) Splits XXIII and XII into landmark numbers
(b) Lists the partial products of each part with each part
(c) Collects 2 C, 7 X and 6 I
(d) Regroups 7 X into L and XX, and 6 I into V and I
(e) Writes CCLXXVI

questions.q: (a) Write the first four landmark numbers of a base-7 system. (b) Write 100 in this system by saying how many of each landmark number it needs. (c) How many symbols does this numeral have altogether?
questions.a: (a) 1, 7, 49 and 343. (b) 100 = 49 + 49 + 1 + 1, so it needs two 49s, no 7s and two 1s. (c) It has 2 + 0 + 2 = 4 symbols.

questions.q:
Write 1000 in a base-6 system by grouping it into landmark numbers, largest first.
(a) List the landmark numbers of the system up to 1296.
(b) Which is the largest landmark number that fits in 1000, how many of it are taken, and what is left?
(c) Group the rest into the smaller landmark numbers.
(d) How many symbols does the numeral have in all?
questions.a: (a) 1, 6, 36, 216 and 1296. (b) 216 is the largest that fits. Four of it make 864, leaving 1000 - 864 = 136. (c) 136 = 3 x 36 + 28, and 28 = 4 x 6 + 4, so three 36s, four 6s and four 1s. (d) 4 + 3 + 4 + 4 = 15 symbols.
s: (b) Takes four 216s and finds 136 left
(c) Groups 136 as three 36s, four 6s and four 1s
(d) Counts 15 symbols

questions.q:
A scribe in an Egyptian grain store stamps his records with a set of carved stamps. His stamp set has symbols only for 1, 10, 100, 1000 and 10,000. On Monday 1,246 sacks of grain arrive and on Tuesday 2,308 sacks. He records each day's count by grouping it into landmark numbers, largest first, and then records the total of the two days.
(a) How many symbols does Monday's record need?
(b) Find the total by regrouping, and say how many of each symbol it needs.
(c) Later the store holds 1,00,000 sacks. Can he stamp this with his set, using at most 9 of any one symbol? What does this show about the Egyptian system as numbers grow larger?
questions.a: (a) 1,246 needs 1 + 2 + 4 + 6 = 13 symbols. (b) The total is 3,554: the 14 ones regroup as 1 ten and 4 ones, giving 3 symbols for 1000, 5 for 100, 5 for 10 and 4 for 1. (c) No. 1,00,000 is ten 10,000s, so he needs a new symbol for 1,00,000. The Egyptians did have symbols up to a crore, but to write larger and larger numbers the system needs an unending sequence of new symbols for higher and higher powers of 10. This is its shortcoming.
s: (a) Finds 13 symbols
(b) Regroups and finds 3,554 as 3, 5, 5 and 4 symbols
(c) Says no, a new symbol is needed, and that ever higher powers of 10 each need a new symbol

questions.q: An Egyptian scribe's record has 13 symbols for 100 and 5 strokes. Regroup it so that no symbol occurs 10 or more times, and write the numeral as the number of each symbol.

questions.q: On the decimal abacus each line stands for a power of 10, and a counter placed above a line counts 5 of that line. Using a counter above the line wherever you can, (a) how is 7 shown on the line for 1? (b) how is 40 shown on the line for 10?

(b) Shows 40 as four counters on the line for 10

questions.q: State the property of the landmark numbers that makes multiplication easy in a number system with a base. Give one product of two Roman landmark numbers for which this property fails.
questions.a: In a number system with a base the landmark numbers are powers of one number, so the product of any two landmark numbers is another landmark number. This fails in the Roman system: for example V x D = 2,500 = MMD, which is not a Roman landmark number.
s: States that the product of two landmark numbers is another landmark number
Gives a Roman product such as V x D = MMD that is not a landmark number

questions.q: A base-5 system uses a for 1, b for 5, c for 25, d for 125 and e for 625. Multiply the numeral 2 c, 3 b, 4 a by c (which is 25), using the distributive property.
questions.a: (2c + 3b + 4a) x c = (2 x c x c) + (3 x b x c) + (4 x a x c). Now c x c = e, b x c = d and a x c = c, so the product is 2 e, 3 d, 4 c.
s: Splits the product using the distributive property
Uses c x c = e, b x c = d and a x c = c
Writes the product 2 e, 3 d, 4 c

questions.q: An Egyptian scribe adds two records. The first has 6 symbols for 1000, 9 for 100, 7 for 10 and 8 strokes. The second has 4 symbols for 1000, 3 for 100, 5 for 10 and 7 strokes. (a) Collect the like symbols. (b) Regroup, starting from the strokes. (c) Write the sum as the number of each symbol.
questions.a: (a) Together there are 10 symbols for 1000, 12 for 100, 12 for 10 and 15 strokes. (b) 15 strokes make 1 symbol for 10 and 5 strokes; 13 tens make 1 for 100 and 3 for 10; 13 hundreds make 1 for 1000 and 3 for 100; 11 thousands make 1 for 10,000 and 1 for 1000. (c) The sum is 1 symbol for 10,000, 1 for 1000, 3 for 100, 3 for 10 and 5 strokes.
s: (a) Collects 10, 12, 12 and 15
(b) Regroups upward from the strokes, carrying 1 each time

questions.q:
On the decimal abacus each line stands for 1, 10, 100 or 1000, and a counter placed above a line counts 5 of that line. Show 2,715 on the abacus by saying what is on each line.
(a) The line for 1000.
(b) The line for 100.
(c) The line for 10.
(d) The line for 1.
questions.a: (a) 2 counters on the line for 1000. (b) 7 hundreds: one counter above the line (500) and 2 counters on the line for 100. (c) 1 counter on the line for 10. (d) 5 ones: one counter above the line for 1 and none on the line.
s: (a) Puts 2 counters on the line for 1000
(b) Puts one counter above and 2 on the line for 100
(c) Puts 1 counter on the line for 10
(d) Puts one counter above and none on the line for 1

questions.q:
On the decimal abacus the lines stand for 1, 10, 100 and 1000, a counter above a line counts 5 of that line, and ten of a line are replaced by one counter on the next line. Add 3846 and 175 by combining the two sides line by line, starting from the line for 1.
(a) How many are there on the line for 1, and what is carried?
(b) Do the same for the lines for 10 and for 100.
(c) Write the sum.
(d) Using a counter above a line wherever you can, how many counters show 3846, and how many show the sum?
(e) A clerk says, 'The sum is the bigger number, so it must need more counters.' Use (d) to decide whether he is right, and say what the number of counters depends on.
questions.a: (a) 6 + 5 = 11 ones, so 1 one stays and 1 ten is carried. (b) Tens: 4 + 7 + 1 = 12, so 2 stay and 1 hundred is carried. Hundreds: 8 + 1 + 1 = 10, so 0 stay and 1 thousand is carried. (c) Thousands: 3 + 1 = 4, so the sum is 4021. (d) 3846 needs 3 + (1 above + 3) + 4 + (1 above + 1) = 13 counters; 4021 needs 4 + 0 + 2 + 1 = 7 counters. (e) He is wrong: the bigger number 4021 needs only 7 counters against 13. The number of counters depends on the digit on each line, not on the size of the number.
s: (a) Finds 11 ones, keeps 1 and carries 1 ten
(b) Finds 12 tens (carry 1) and 10 hundreds (carry 1)
(c) Writes 4021
(d) Finds 13 counters for 3846 and 7 for 4021
(e) Says the clerk is wrong, since counters depend on the digits, not the size

questions.q: In later times the number system of ancient Mesopotamia became a place value system with which base?

Consider the following statements.
I. The landmark number positions of the Mayan system are 1, 20 and 360.
II. The Chinese rod numerals form a base-10 (decimal) system.

questions.q: Write 250 as a sum of a multiple of 60 and a number of ones, and write it as a Mesopotamian base-60 numeral in the form (groups of 60) (ones).

questions.q: True or false: A Mayan numeral with 1 in the third level and the shell placeholder in the two lower levels stands for the same number as the numeral 1, 0, 0 in a true base-20 place value system. Give the reason or the correct statement.
questions.a: False. The Mayan third level stands for 360, so the Mayan numeral is 360. In a true base-20 system the third position stands for 20 x 20 = 400, so 1, 0, 0 is 400.

questions.q: In Chinese rod numerals the units and the hundreds are written in zong form. In which form are the tens and the thousands written, and why were the two forms alternated?
questions.a: The tens and thousands are written in heng form. Alternating the forms makes the neighbouring places easy to tell apart, so that a digit is not confused with the digit next to it.
s: Names the heng form for tens and thousands
Says the forms alternate so that neighbouring places can be told apart

questions.q: In Chinese rod numerals the units and hundreds are written in zong form and the tens and thousands in heng form, and a skipped place is left blank. (a) A rod numeral shows, from left to right, 5 in heng form, 7 in zong form, 2 in heng form and 8 in zong form, with no blanks. What number is it? (b) Another rod numeral shows only two digits: 4 in zong form, then 1 in zong form, the 1 being the units. Why must a place have been skipped between them, and what is the number if exactly one place was skipped? (c) Why is a blank still less clear than the 0 digit of the Hindu system?
questions.a: (a) 5 thousands, 7 hundreds, 2 tens and 8 ones, so 5728. (b) The place next to the units, the tens, is written in heng form, so a zong 4 cannot be in the tens place; the tens place is blank and the 4 is in the hundreds place, giving 401. (c) A blank does not clearly show how many places are empty, but the Hindu system writes a 0 digit in every empty place with a single digit in each position, so its numerals cannot be misread.
s: (a) Reads the numeral as 5728
(b) Says two zongs side by side mean the heng (tens) place is empty, and gives 401
(c) Says a blank does not show how many places are empty, while a 0 digit fills every empty place

questions.q:
The chapter asks how we would write numbers with Hindu-style digits if we used a base other than 10. Write the number 60 in base 4 and in base 3.
(a) List the landmark numbers of base 4 that are not more than 60, and group 60 with them, largest first.
(b) Write the base-4 numeral.
(c) Group 60 with the landmark numbers 1, 3, 9 and 27 of base 3, and write the base-3 numeral.
(d) What does each 0 in the base-3 numeral do?
questions.a: (a) The landmark numbers are 1, 4 and 16, and 60 = 3 x 16 + 3 x 4 + 0 x 1. (b) The base-4 numeral is 330. (c) 60 = 2 x 27 + 0 x 9 + 2 x 3 + 0 x 1, so the base-3 numeral is 2020. (d) Each 0 is a placeholder showing an empty place: the 0 next to the left 2 shows there are no 9s, and the last 0 shows there are no 1s.
s: (a) Lists 1, 4, 16 and groups 60 = 3 x 16 + 3 x 4
(b) Writes 330
(c) Groups 60 = 2 x 27 + 2 x 3 and writes 2020
(d) Says each 0 holds an empty place (the 9s and the 1s)

questions.q:
In the later Mesopotamian base-60 system, a numeral for 9,000 was written without a placeholder at the end.
(a) Group 9,000 into powers of 60.
(b) Write the numeral as a scribe who used no placeholder at the end would write it, in the form (groups of 3600) (groups of 60).
(c) If a reader takes the last group as the 1s, what number does he read?
(d) Why could the reader not tell that the numeral stands for 9,000?
(e) How does the 0 digit of the Hindu number system avoid this problem?
questions.a: (a) 9,000 = 2 x 3600 + 30 x 60 + 0 x 1. (b) The scribe writes (2) (30) and leaves the last place unmarked. (c) Taking 30 as the 1s and 2 as the 60s, he reads 2 x 60 + 30 = 150. (d) The placeholder was mainly used in the middle of a numeral and not at the end, so nothing showed that the 1s place was empty. (e) In the Hindu system a 0 digit is written in every empty place, even at the end, so 9000 and 150 look different.
s: (b) Writes (2) (30)
(c) Reads it as 2 x 60 + 30 = 150
(d) Says the placeholder was not used at the end of a numeral
(e) Says the Hindu 0 fills every empty place, even at the end

questions.q:
A museum card shows a Mayan numeral with three levels. The level for 360 holds 3, the level for 20 holds the shell-shaped placeholder for zero, and the level for 1 holds 4. A visitor then reads the digits 3, 0 and 4 as a Hindu numeral.
(a) Find the value of the Mayan numeral.
(b) What number do the digits 3, 0, 4 stand for in the Hindu system, and how much smaller is it than the Mayan value?
(c) On a worn copy of the card the shell has rubbed off, and a reader sees only two levels: 3 above 4. What value does he get, and what job did the shell do?
questions.a: (a) 3 x 360 + 0 x 20 + 4 = 1084. (b) In the Hindu system the digits stand for 304, which is 1084 - 304 = 780 less. (c) He takes 3 as the 20s and 4 as the 1s and gets 3 x 20 + 4 = 64. The shell marked the empty 20s level, which kept the 3 in the 360s level.
s: (b) Finds 304 and the difference 780
(c) Finds 3 x 20 + 4 = 64 and says the shell held the empty 20s level so that the 3 stayed in the 360s level

questions.q:
Two Mesopotamian clerks record grain in the base-60 system. The first entry is written (1) (5) (20). For the second entry, which is 3,605, an early scribe leaves a blank between the groups (1) and (5) because no placeholder is used. A reader who misses the blank reads the second entry as (1) (5).
(a) Find the value of the first entry.
(b) Find the value the careless reader gets for the second entry, and how far it is from 3,605.
(c) Later Mesopotamians marked an empty place with a placeholder symbol. Write the second entry with the placeholder shown as 0, in the form (groups of 3600) (groups of 60) (ones), and say why the reader can no longer get the wrong value.
questions.a: (a) 1 x 3600 + 5 x 60 + 20 = 3,920. (b) (1) (5) is read as 1 x 60 + 5 = 65, which is 3,605 - 65 = 3,540 too small. (c) 3,605 = 1 x 3600 + 0 x 60 + 5, so it is written (1) (0) (5). The placeholder fills the empty 60s place in the middle, so the 1 can only be in the 3600s place.
s: (b) Finds 65 and the difference 3,540
(c) Writes (1) (0) (5) and says the placeholder fixes the 1 in the 3600s place
